0e15bbc3209b57:
The most personal science of all

Of all the sciences, biology is perhaps the most personal: it doesn't just study "things out there" — it studies you. Your cells, your DNA, your body's systems, and why you look (and don't look) like your parents, all of that is biology.

This course is built mostly around reading, just like Introduction to Psychology — because understanding life at the cellular and genetic level requires the same kind of attention as any serious science, not a 3-minute summary.

The course map

  • Fundamentals (classes 2-4): what biology is, the cell, and DNA — the most basic pieces of every living thing.
  • How life changes and organizes itself (classes 5-7): evolution, species classification, and how living things get energy.
  • You and other living things (classes 8-11): the human body, heredity, ecosystems and the microscopic world.
  • Applied biology and wrap-up (classes 12-13): modern biotechnology, and your own mind map of everything you learned.
💡 How to read each class well: read it through once, then read it again slowly noting what surprised you, and before moving on answer the reflection quest with your pet — explaining something in your own words is the best way to know if you truly understood it.

09a5effc050ce4:
A simple definition, a huge field

Biology is defined as the science that studies living things — their structure, function, growth, origin, evolution and distribution. It's such a broad field that it splits into many specialized branches.

Some main branches

  • Botany: the study of plants.
  • Zoology: the study of animals.
  • Microbiology: the study of microscopic organisms.
  • Genetics: the study of heredity and genes.
  • Ecology: the study of how living things interact with each other and their environment.

What makes something "alive"?

It's not as obvious as it sounds. Biologists generally agree that a living thing must meet several characteristics at once:

  1. Organization: it's made up of one or more cells.
  2. Metabolism: it transforms energy to keep itself running.
  3. Homeostasis: it keeps its internal environment stable.
  4. Growth and development: it changes and develops over time.
  5. Reproduction: it can produce offspring.
  6. Response to stimuli: it reacts to its environment.
  7. Evolution: its populations change across generations.
🔥 An odd case: a virus doesn't meet all these criteria on its own — it has no metabolism of its own, it needs a host cell to reproduce. That's why scientists still debate whether viruses should be considered "alive" in the strict sense.

1300a6d0ebf32d: Every living thing, from the simplest bacterium to you, is made of cells. What they are, their two major types, and their most important parts.
0bdb4ffa0c8b55:
Cell theory

One of the most important principles in all of biology is cell theory: all living things are made up of one or more cells, the cell is the basic unit of structure and function in life, and every cell comes from a pre-existing cell.

Two major types of cells

Prokaryotic cells

Simpler and evolutionarily older. They have no defined nucleus — their genetic material floats freely inside the cell. Bacteria are prokaryotes.

Eukaryotic cells

More complex, with a membrane-bound nucleus that holds their DNA, and specialized internal structures called organelles. Animals, plants, fungi and protists are made of eukaryotic cells — including you.

🔬 Some key organelles of a eukaryotic cell:
  • Nucleus: holds the DNA, "the command center."
  • Mitochondria: generates the cell's energy (the "ATP") — which is why it's called "the cell's power plant."
  • Cell membrane: controls what goes in and out.
  • Ribosomes: build proteins following the DNA's instructions.

A scale that's hard to imagine

Your body has an estimated 37 trillion cells. Every single one of them came from the division of one original cell — the fertilized egg from which you began to exist.

💡 When we talk about the human body in module 8, you'll see how groups of specialized cells form tissues, tissues form organs, and organs form the systems that keep you alive.

1c19703864d4e4:
A massive organization problem

It's estimated there are between 8 and 10 million species on Earth (and most haven't even been formally described yet). To be able to study them, talk about them without confusion, and understand their relationships, biology needs a classification system.

Linnaeus and the binomial system

Swedish naturalist Carl Linnaeus (1707–1778) created the system we still use today: every species gets a two-part scientific name (genus + species), always in Latin. For example, humans are Homo sapiens, the domestic dog is Canis lupus familiaris.

🐺 Why use Latin: it's a "dead" language that doesn't change over time or vary between countries — so a scientist in Japan and another in Mexico know exactly which species the other is talking about, no matter what language they normally speak.

The levels of the hierarchy

From most general to most specific: Domain → Kingdom → Phylum → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species. Each level groups organisms that are increasingly similar to each other.

The three domains of life

Today science recognizes three major domains: Bacteria, Archaea (single-celled organisms that often live in extreme environments) and Eukarya (everything with nucleated cells: animals, plants, fungi and protists).

💡 This system isn't just organization — it reflects real evolutionary relationships. Two species in the same genus share a more recent common ancestor than two species in different genera.

0abfecb5377e90: Photosynthesis and cellular respiration: how energy moves
1c863c36d63210: The two complementary processes that explain how the sun's energy ends up, literally, inside every one of your cells.
1660bdec0bee8a:
Where all of life's energy comes from

Almost all the energy living things on Earth use ultimately comes from the Sun. The question is: how does solar energy go from light to something a cell can use?

Photosynthesis: light → sugar

Plants, algae and some bacteria carry out photosynthesis: they use the energy from sunlight, water and carbon dioxide (CO₂) to make glucose (sugar) and release oxygen as a byproduct.

🌱 The simplified equation: Carbon dioxide + Water + Sunlight → Glucose + Oxygen. Every time you breathe in oxygen, you owe that air, indirectly, to some plant's or alga's photosynthesis.

Cellular respiration: sugar → usable energy

But glucose on its own isn't "ready to use" energy for the cell. Almost all living things (including plants themselves) carry out cellular respiration: they take that glucose and oxygen and convert them into usable energy (ATP), releasing CO₂ and water as byproducts.

A perfectly complementary cycle

Notice something elegant: the products of photosynthesis (glucose and oxygen) are exactly what cellular respiration needs, and the products of cellular respiration (CO₂ and water) are exactly what photosynthesis needs. It's a closed loop that sustains life on the planet.

💡 This happens in the mitochondria — the "power plant" organelle you saw in class 3. Every one of your cells is, right now, carrying out cellular respiration to keep you running on energy.

1e0b8f871fed11: How trillions of cells organize into tissues, organs and systems to keep you alive — a general overview you can dig deeper into with this school's 3D game.
05aeaf94e67804:
From cell to system

Remember the organizational scale from class 3: similar cells group into tissues (like muscle tissue or nervous tissue), tissues organize into organs (like the heart or the liver), and organs working together toward a common goal form systems.

A quick review of the main systems

  • Skeletal-muscular system: 206 bones and more than 600 muscles give you structure and movement.
  • Circulatory system: the heart pumps blood through about 100,000 km of blood vessels, carrying oxygen and nutrients to every cell.
  • Respiratory system: lungs that exchange oxygen for carbon dioxide with every breath.
  • Digestive system: converts food into nutrients cells can use.
  • Nervous system: the brain and a network of nerves that coordinate everything else, at speeds up to 120 meters per second.
🫀 A fact that connects to Medicine: if you took (or are taking) the Introduction to Medicine course, you'll remember William Harvey discovering the heart is a pump — that's exactly the circulatory system you just read about, seen from history instead of biology.

Nothing works in isolation

No system works alone: when you run, the nervous system coordinates the movement, the muscular system carries it out, the respiratory and circulatory systems bring more oxygen, and the digestive system supplies the stored energy. The human body is, literally, teamwork at the cellular level.

06f21029213075: Why you look like your parents but aren't identical to them — the basic rules Gregor Mendel discovered by studying pea plants.
15c96efcec65a2:
The monk who discovered the rules of heredity

Gregor Mendel (1822–1884), an Austrian monk, spent years growing and crossbreeding thousands of pea plants, meticulously noting traits like flower color and seed shape. From that work came the basic laws of genetic inheritance.

Alleles: different versions of the same gene

Every gene can have slightly different versions called alleles. You inherit one allele of each gene from each of your parents — one from your mother, one from your father.

🌱 Mendel's experiment: when crossing purple-flowered plants with white-flowered plants, the first generation was all purple — but crossing that generation with itself, white flowers appeared again, in a ratio of 1 in 4. This revealed there are "dominant" alleles (purple) and "recessive" alleles (white) — the recessive one only shows up if two matching copies are inherited.

Sexual reproduction: the source of variety

Sexual reproduction (unlike asexual reproduction, where the offspring is an identical genetic copy) mixes the genetic material of two parents, generating new combinations every time — which is why no sibling (except identical twins) is genetically identical to another.

💡 This genetic variety isn't a minor detail: it's the "raw material" that the natural selection you saw in class 5 acts on — without genetic variation, evolution would have nothing to work with.

0311fcdb1ca0f0:
What is an ecosystem?

An ecosystem is the set of all living things (the "biological community") in an area, together with the non-living factors of its environment (water, soil, climate, light), and all the interactions between them.

Food chains and food webs

Energy moves through an ecosystem via food chains: producers (plants, which photosynthesize) are eaten by primary consumers (herbivores), which are eaten by secondary consumers (carnivores), and so on. In real nature, these chains intertwine into much more complex food webs.

🐺 A real, famous case: when wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone National Park in 1995 (after having been wiped out decades earlier), it didn't just change the deer population — it changed the behavior of the rivers. Fewer deer eating vegetation along the rivers let trees grow back, which stabilized the banks and changed the water's course. This chain effect is called a "trophic cascade."

Relationships between species

Species interact in very different ways: predation (one hunts another), competition (they compete for the same resource), mutualistic symbiosis (both benefit, like bees and flowers), and parasitism (one benefits at the other's expense).

💡 Yellowstone's lesson repeats in many ecosystems: removing or adding a single species can have effects that ripple through the whole system in ways that aren't always obvious at first.

051e1e9956878d:
Biotechnology isn't new

When you hear "biotechnology" you might think of ultramodern labs — but humanity has been using living organisms as a tool for thousands of years, long before understanding the science behind it.

🍞 Ancient biotechnology: bread, beer and wine exist thanks to fermentation — a biological process carried out by yeasts (microscopic fungi) that humanity used for millennia without knowing microorganisms were involved.

From artificial selection to genetic engineering

For centuries, humans practiced artificial selection: deliberately choosing which plants or animals reproduced, based on desired traits (more fruit, more milk, better flavor). Modern corn, for example, is radically different from its wild ancestor because of artificial selection accumulated over thousands of years.

Modern biotechnology took a leap with the ability to manipulate DNA directly: insulin produced by genetically modified bacteria (it used to be extracted from animal pancreases), lab-produced vaccines, and — as you saw if you took Introduction to Medicine — tools like CRISPR for editing genes with precision.

Current applications

Today biotechnology is used in medicine (medications, gene therapies), agriculture (crops resistant to pests or drought), and even in industry (enzymes produced by microorganisms for detergents, biofuels).

💡 Biotechnology, as you saw with CRISPR in the Medicine course, also raises important ethical questions: what limits should gene editing have? These are questions science alone can't answer — they also need social reflection.

1a73cde597ffce:
The molecule of heredity

DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is a double-helix-shaped molecule — two intertwined strands, like a spiral staircase — that holds the instructions for building and keeping a living thing running.

An alphabet of only 4 letters

DNA is made up of combinations of just 4 chemical bases: Adenine (A), Thymine (T), Cytosine (C) and Guanine (G). The order in which these 4 letters repeat, across millions of positions, is literally the "code" that determines everything from your eye color to how your cells function.

📖 A useful analogy: if a person's complete DNA (the genome) were a book, it would have more than 3 billion "letters" — the equivalent of hundreds of entire encyclopedias, all stored inside every one of your cells.

What is a gene?

A gene is a specific segment of DNA that contains the instructions for making a particular protein (or regulating some function). Humans have approximately 20,000 genes — surprisingly few, considering the entire complexity of the human body.

DNA vs. chromosome vs. gene

To avoid mixing them up: DNA is the molecule itself; a chromosome is DNA packaged and organized (humans have 46, in 23 pairs); a gene is a specific section of that DNA with one concrete instruction.

💡 99.9% of human DNA is identical between any two people on the planet — the remaining 0.1% is what accounts for all the individual variation you see between people.
